turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you, Doc. Yeah, so, what brings me in... man, it's work. I'm a construction manager, and lately, I just can't keep on track. Like, I'll start a safety briefing with the crew or sit down for a plan review, and I'm trying really, really hard to pay attention. But honestly, within a couple of minutes, my mind is completely off on three other job problems. 

Which reminds me, we've got this massive issue with the drywall guys right now on the new site. They keep leaving their trash everywhere, and I told their foreman, I said, if you don't clean up these Monster Energy cans, I'm throwing you off the site. It's a tripping hazard, you know? Someone's gonna twist an ankle. My brother-in-law twisted his ankle last Thanksgiving playing touch football in the yard and he was out of work for like two months, had to wear this giant plastic boot... 

Anyway, sorry, what was I saying? Right, the plan reviews. My mind just wanders off like that to all the other fires I need to put out, and because of it, I end up missing things in the blueprints or the safety protocols that I know I should have caught. It's getting really bad.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient reports missing details in blueprints and safety protocols that he knows he should have caught.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention during safety briefings and plan reviews, losing focus within minutes despite trying hard.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient's mind easily wanders to unrelated thoughts and other job problems, demonstrating distractibility both in his description and his tangential speech during the response.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your life, did you have these same struggles with staying focused and getting distracted when you were a child in school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, man, 100 percent. Back in elementary school, it was the exact same thing. My teachers were already calling my parents, telling them I couldn't stay in my seat to save my life. I was always talking out of turn, just blurting stuff out. 

Which is funny because my youngest, Tommy, he's doing the exact same thing right now. He's seven, and his teacher actually lets them sit on these giant rubber yoga balls instead of regular chairs. It's supposed to help them get their energy out, I guess? I tried sitting on one of those at the site trailer a couple weeks ago because my lower back was killing me from hauling some lumber, and I swear I nearly busted my tailbone. The thing just slipped right out from under me. I had a bruise the size of a grapefruit for a week, couldn't even drive my truck without wincing... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, me in school. Yeah, so besides the talking, I was always losing my homework, too. It would just completely disappear from my backpack. And whenever we had an assignment, I'd just rush right through the directions before I even really understood what I was supposed to be doing. I just wanted to get it done and get outside, you know? But yeah, the teachers were always on my case about it.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient states he would rush through directions before understanding what he was supposed to do, indicating difficulty following instructions.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient mentions he was always losing his homework and it would disappear from his backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient confirms childhood distractibility and demonstrates it in the present by going on a tangent and losing his train of thought ('Wait, what were we talking about?').
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports that his teachers told his parents he couldn't stay in his seat.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient notes he was 'always talking out of turn'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states he was 'just blurting stuff out' in class.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from the trouble with focus, do you still find yourself feeling like you have a 'motor' running inside you, or do you struggle to stay still in situations where you're expected to be quiet, like during meetings or while sitting in your truck?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, the motor thing... absolutely. It's like I can't just sit there. In these big site meetings, you know, where everybody else can just sit through the whole hour-long thing without moving a muscle, I'm always the guy standing up. I'll get up to grab a coffee, or I'll step outside to "check on a delivery," or I'll just make up some excuse to move around. 

Speaking of coffee, they changed the brand in the site trailer last week, and man, it is awful. It tastes like burnt dirt. I told the office manager, I said, 'Look, I know we're trying to cut costs because of the steel tariffs, but we can't be drinking this sludge.' My buddy Mike, he works over at the union hall, and he gets this amazing local roast delivered right to his desk. He actually gave me a bag for Christmas last year, wrapped it in this ridiculous snowman paper that his wife picked out. She's super crafty, always making these little wreaths out of pinecones and stuff...

Sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? But yeah, staying in my seat during meetings? Practically impossible for me. I just gotta be up and moving.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about coffee, his friend Mike, and Christmas wrapping paper before catching himself.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states that it is practically impossible for him to stay in his seat during meetings and that he frequently makes excuses to stand up and move around.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient confirms feeling like he has a 'motor' running inside him, stating 'the motor thing... absolutely.'

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over the last six months, would you say that your struggles with getting distracted and losing focus are more frequent and problematic for you than your struggles with feeling restless and having to move around?
turns.patient_response:
Man, the last six months... I don't even know if I could pick which one is worse, honestly. They both just mess me up every single day. Six months ago, we were just starting the foundation on that big commercial build off Route 9, so it's all been a blur anyway. 

Speaking of Route 9, they've had that right lane closed for roadwork since, like, April, and it is an absolute nightmare. I was stuck in traffic there for forty-five minutes last Tuesday just trying to get to the hardware store for some masonry drill bits. And the guy in front of me had this bumper sticker that said "My other ride is a tractor" and I was just thinking, who even drives a tractor around here? We're in the suburbs. My uncle had a farm upstate when I was a kid, though, and he let me drive his big green John Deere once. I was maybe twelve? I accidentally put it in the wrong gear and ran it right over my aunt's prize-winning tomato bushes. She was so mad she wouldn't talk to me for the rest of the summer. Made me eat dinner on the porch...

Wait, sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, which one is more of a problem. Yeah, I honestly couldn't tell you. The zoning out and the having to move around, they're both just... always happening. I haven't really noticed one being worse than the other, they're both pretty bad.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient confirms that 'zoning out' and losing focus are daily problems.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient agrees that struggles with getting distracted happen every single day.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms that feeling restless and 'having to move around' are constant issues.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic about traffic, a tractor, and an uncle's farm before having to ask what the original question was.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about the last six months, have you found yourself frequently blurting out answers before questions are completed, or struggling to wait your turn in conversations or group activities?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah, all the time. I just cut people off constantly because I think I already know exactly where their question is going. So I just jump in and answer way too fast. 

Like the other day with my lead electrician, Dave. Dave is a great guy, but man, he talks slower than molasses. He was asking me about the wiring for the second floor, and I just blurted out the answer before he was even halfway done. But he... well, speaking of Dave, he drives this beat-up old Chevy Silverado, right? Thing has like three hundred thousand miles on it and sounds like a broken lawnmower. He refuses to get rid of it because he says they don't make the transmissions like they used to. Which I get, honestly. I had an '04 Ford that I drove into the ground. Best truck I ever owned. Had this custom tool rack in the back that my dad welded for me before he moved down to Florida. He's down in Tampa now, playing golf three days a week and complaining about the humidity. He keeps trying to get me and the kids to come down for Disney, but the ticket prices these days are just highway robbery...

Wait, I'm doing it again. Sorry. What was I saying? Right, blurting things out. Yeah, so with Dave, because I jumped the gun and answered too fast, I realized a second later that I totally missed the important part of his question that he hadn't even said yet. He was actually asking about a major issue with the HVAC ducts, not the wire gauge. So yeah, I do that a lot. I just can't seem to wait for people to finish their sentences.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly confirms blurting out answers, stating he jumps in and answers 'way too fast' before questions are finished.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to frequently interrupting others, noting 'I just cut people off constantly.'
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient demonstrates tangentiality during the response, drifting from a story about his coworker to trucks, his father, and Disney ticket prices before catching himself.
